paras: The killing of Ernest Brown was the fatal shooting of a Black man by George Alford, a farmer near Rome, Georgia, in early August 1920. Alford accused Brown of an attempted assault on his wife, and the coroner cleared him after an inquest. The Associated Press carried the farmer's exoneration in white dailies the next day, and the Associated Negro Press relayed a shorter version to Black weeklies later in the month.

Alford was described as "a prominent farmer of the Chuilo district" near Rome. According to the Associated Press, Brown was alleged to have attempted an assault on Alford's wife on Sunday, the day before the shooting.

Brown was shot and killed early on the morning of the AP dispatch, dated Rome, August 2. In the account given as evidence at the inquest, Brown boasted of the alleged assault to Black friends, returned to the scene, and drew a knife when Alford approached him, whereupon the farmer killed him. The Black-press brief said only that Brown was "shot and instantly killed" by the farmer and mentioned no knife.

The AP reported that Alford "was exonerated by the coroner." The Black-press version specified that a coroner's jury acquitted the farmer "after hearing the farmer's testimony." No report of an arrest, grand jury action or trial appears in the coverage.

White coverage was an Associated Press dispatch that ran on August 3 in the Richmond Times-Dispatch under the headline "FARMER IS EXONERATED FOR SLAYING A NEGRO" and in the Alexandria Gazette as "FARMER EXONERAED." Both papers added a subhead saying Brown had boasted of "His Attack on Alford's Wife," treating the alleged assault as fact, and both named the farmer.

Black papers received the story more than two weeks later as a three-sentence item that left the farmer unnamed and called the assault the farmer's accusation. On August 21 it appeared in the Savannah Tribune, in the Washington Bee's "News Notes," and in the Phoenix Tribune's "Daily Happenings in Georgia," credited to the Associated Negro Press. Unlike the AP text, it stated that the acquittal followed the farmer's own testimony. The Dallas Express ran it on August 28 under "SHOT AND KILLED NEGRO— ACQUITTED." In the Washington Bee the item sat beside a Jacksonville report of a Black hotel porter tried on a charge of attempted assault on "a young white woman" and sentenced to ninety days on the city prison farm.

The accounts disagree on the date. The AP, filed the same day, placed the killing early on Monday, August 2, while the Black-press brief said "last Wednesday morning" under datelines that ranged from August 5 to August 26. The contemporaneous AP report is the more specific source on timing, though the knife and the boasting it describes rest on inquest evidence that the Black press attributed to the farmer himself.

reader.title: Killing of Ernest Brown
bases: A single named farmer shot Brown in a private confrontation over an accusation; no mob, band, posse or officers appear in any report (A1, A2, A3).

The Associated Press report in the white press (A1, A2) and the Associated Negro Press brief in the Black press (A3, A5) agree that a prominent farmer near Rome shot and killed Ernest Brown over an alleged attempted assault on his wife and was cleared by the coroner; the two differ in date and detail, which suggests separate transmission.

accounts.label: Inquest evidence as reported by the Associated Press
accounts.gist: Brown boasted of the alleged assault to Black friends, returned to the scene, and drew a knife when Alford approached; the farmer then killed him and the coroner exonerated him.

accounts.label: Associated Negro Press brief
accounts.gist: A prominent farmer shot and instantly killed Brown 'last Wednesday morning', accusing him of an attempted assault on his wife; a coroner's jury acquitted the farmer after hearing only his testimony. No knife is mentioned.

framing.detail: AP headlines stressed the farmer's exoneration and a subhead said Brown had boasted of 'His Attack on Alford's Wife', presenting the alleged assault and the inquest account as established.
A three-sentence wire brief without comment, framing the assault as the farmer's accusation and noting the acquittal rested on 'the farmer's testimony'.
The Dallas Express headlined the brief 'SHOT AND KILLED NEGRO— ACQUITTED', putting the killing and acquittal side by side.

versions.value: Early morning of Aug. 2 (AP dispatch dated Aug. 2; the Alexandria copy dated Aug. 3)

conflicts.note: The AP report was filed the day of the killing and gives specifics; the Black-press brief reached weeklies two to three weeks later with shifting datelines, so its 'last Wednesday' is probably relative to an earlier, unstated date.
